title: SIU clears police officer in truck crash: Driver of stolen car died during chase
article: The Special Investigations Unit has cleared the police officer who chased a blue pickup before its driver lost control, crashed and died near the Cummings Bridge on Canada Day.
"There are no reasonable grounds to believe that an Ottawa Police Service officer acted criminally during a pursuit on July 1," said the SIU's director, Peter A. Tinsley.
The SIU is called in each time police are involved in the death or serious injury of a civilian.
Five investigators, including two forensic specialists, interviewed witnesses and police officers after the July 1 crash.
The investigation revealed that Stephane Drouin, 19, was driving dangerously throughout the afternoon just before the crash, which injured his three passengers.
"That pattern of driving takes away from the conclusion that the collision and Mr. Drouin's death were precipitated by, or causally linked to, the involved officer's pursuit," said Mr. Tinsley.
Mr. Drouin was driving a stolen blue Dodge Dakota Sport truck at speeds in excess of 100 km/h across the bridge, according to a witness.

He couldn't make the curve at the beginning of Montreal Road, hit an old-fashioned street lamp and then a wooden hydro pole before crashing into a traffic light post at the corner of Montgomery Street. He died of injuries the next day in hospital.
The SIU's investigation found the stolen truck had not stopped for police in the Byward Market earlier in the day. Someone had complained about the way the truck was being driven.
"They chased him for squealing his tires in a parking lot," said Christine Donell, a close friend of Mr. Drouin's.
The officer in the Market broadcast the truck's description over the police radio.

Another officer, travelling west on Rideau Street, first saw the truck at the corner of Wurtemburg Street, where he had to swerve to avoid hitting it. The officer turned on his lights and siren and chased the truck until it crashed, 500 metres east.
"It was an extremely short pursuit," said Rose Hong, the SIU's spokeswoman. She said it was one of the factors that cleared the officer.
Mr. Drouin pulled "a stupid stunt," said Ms. Donell. She said her friend "had run away from the police before and thought he could get away with it again."
She said the police were wrong in chasing Mr. Drouin. "The police could have chased him to another area where he could have come to a stop, instead of forcing him off the road."
Melad Botros was one of the 200 people on the Montreal Road sidewalk at 5 p.m. that day. He wrote in a letter to the Citizen that he witnessed the pursuit from beginning to end.
He agrees with the SIU's conclusions.
"The person was driving recklessly. The officer was not at fault," said Mr. Botros.
"(The driver) had no reason not to pull over. He thought it was like a video game," he said.
Mr. Drouin did not hold a driver's licence.
This is the second SIU investigation that has found Ottawa police officers not liable for the death of a civilian.
Three weeks ago, the SIU concluded that the death of a cyclist in the Byward Market was "unavoidable."
Benoit Aube, 38, was hit by a slow-moving police tactical unit van after he swerved into its path.
